source.title: WriteSAE: Sparse Autoencoders for Recurrent State

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study extends sparse-dictionary feature analysis to recurrent-model cache writes and reports feature geometry and causal replacement results in several recurrent architectures. It does not reproduce the toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The paper measures sparse-autoencoder atoms, their alignment with native writes, and downstream effects of replacing writes. It does not test toy networks with more features than dimensions, neuron polysemanticity, or whether features overlap because of capacity pressure. Omitted results about deliberately induced generation changes, SAE training ablations, and cited results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains sparse dictionaries (WriteSAE) on matrix cache writes of recurrent LLMs. It reports whether sparse atoms can be recovered that align with and causally replace native writes, across five architectures and three Qwen3.5 scales, plus cross-seed atom identity. This bears on V4 (a dictionary recovers sparse features in real models) and V5 (stability of dictionary features) in a new setting. It does not use toy models or neuron-level polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a rank-1 SAE atom can often replace a single rank-1 cache write, clearest in Gated DeltaNet, and that the replacement test transfers to Mamba-2. They attribute the 4B chance-level result to a reconstruction-vs-write-alignment training-objective gap, and the DeltaNet failure to the lack of gating. They say the register/bundle class, not individual atoms, is the unit that reproduces across seeds. Their claim that RWKV-7 atoms beat deletion at population scale is not backed by a reported number; Table 6 shows 45.3%.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on recurrent cache states and tests replacement of native writes; it does not use the toy-model optimization and superposition measurements of the original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Host architecture and write rule; Qwen3.5 scale and layer/head; DeltaNet TopK setting; SAE seed. The paper also reports that replacement can fail despite high cosine alignment in ungated DeltaNet.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine alignment to the native write does not predict substitution success. GDN shows Pearson r=0.19 (p=0.08); Mamba-2 shows r=0.008. Bundles replace writes about as well as registers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Causal replaceability of SAE atoms is independent of their geometric alignment to the model's native write.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank-2 decoder atoms give parity or only a small gain over rank-1 for replacing rank-1 GDN writes (+0.06pp perplexity; Cliff's δ=-0.028).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary atom rank should match the host write rank.

record.problems: The central causal replacement result is concentrated in selected recurrent cells; the study reports chance-level replacement at Qwen3.5-4B L12 H8 and DeltaNet L12 H8 despite other positive measurements. Individual atom identity is highly seed-specific. The experiments do not test the toy-model dimensional-capacity conditions in the claim.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted generation steering, cache erasure, newline-rate interventions, and SAE training-objective ablations because they do not measure the listed feature-superposition or canonical-unit claims. Also omitted cited findings and values used only to select settings.

untested.parts: No toy models, no features-vs-dimensions manipulation, no sparsity-dependent transition or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-competition analysis.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Features spreading across neurons; residual-stream SAEs in transformer LLMs; whether recovered atoms reflect superposition rather than reconstruction structure.
Completeness of the dictionary and whether any basis is canonical. Dependence on SAE objective is shown only in an ablation (see missing).
Intrinsic dimensionality of features. Rank-1 vs rank-2 atoms concern matching the write rank, not feature dimensionality.

missing.what: Replacement test on all 15 firing L9 heads: mean 89.3% ± 2.6%, range 82.6–93.2%. Shows the main cell is not cherry-picked.
missing.locator: Section 3.2 'All L9 heads'; App. F.1, Table 12

missing.what: Partition counts depend on the SAE objective and k. JumpReLU gives 1,259/773 register/bundle vs BatchTopK 222/94; the k-sweep gives 67, 76 and 155 registers at k=16/32/64.
missing.locator: App. B Table 5; App. G.1 Table 15

missing.what: Mamba-2 single-cell replacement 82.85% vs flat-SAE+SVD 76.30%. Superseded by the 88.08% population sweep.

record.verdict_notes: The link to superposition is indirect. The paper cites superposition theory as motivation but measures dictionary atoms' alignment with, and causal substitutability for, cache writes, not overlap from capacity pressure. V4 verdicts therefore rest on recovering sparse dictionary atoms in recurrent LLM states. Reader labels mislinked r19 to V4; it is corrected to V5.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model test of more features than dimensions, feature interference, or the claimed sparsity-dependent superposition transition and geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity or of dedicated versus shared neuron dimensions.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising through other mechanisms, or whether polysemanticity alone evidences superposition.
Tests sparse dictionary features in recurrent cache states, not feature spreading across neurons, general LLM prevalence, or residual-stream SAEs as a whole.
Reports cross-seed feature identity and class stability, but does not establish whether the dictionary is complete or whether any feature basis is canonical.
Rank-1 versus rank-2 decoder atoms are compared for cache-write replacement; the study does not test the intrinsic dimensionality of superposed features.
